strengths: Addresses a novel and important problem: interactive 4D world generation with environmental dynamics from a single image, extending static 3D world generation into temporally evolving scenes.

Proposes an efficient pipeline combining Eulerian motion estimation, geometry-aware Kabsch-based alignment, a compact hash-based global motion field, and bidirectional propagation, enabling low-latency updates (~12s per expansion) and real-time rendering.

The geometry-aware alignment and bidirectional propagation are well motivated and supported by ablations: improved local/global motion consistency (MCA 0.074, FMV 0.29, cosine 0.91), and a large reduction in boundary holes (9.8% to 0.9%).

Quantitative results show competitive VBench temporal metrics, best PhysReal score, and substantially lower runtime than video-generation and 4D-scene baselines; the human 2AFC study generally supports the approach.
The method is clearly organized, with an algorithmic summary and supplementary implementation details; using publicly available pretrained models supports reproducibility of several components.
The authors acknowledge limitations on rigid-body motion and outline future extension to object-centric dynamics, which is appropriate for the stated scope.
weaknesses: The core technical step of lifting 2D Eulerian flow to 3D scene flow and aligning flow vectors with Kabsch is under-specified; it is unclear how scale, depth ambiguity, and translation are resolved, which weakens confidence in the geometric soundness of the alignment module.

Despite claiming improved 3D consistency as a key advantage, the evaluation lacks direct quantitative metrics for multi-view/3D geometric consistency; comparisons against video generation baselines are on a different task and may not be fully fair or informative.

The GPT-based PhysReal metric is proprietary and inconsistently described (GPT-5.5 in the main text vs. GPT-4o in the supplement), which hurts reproducibility; some human preference results (e.g., vs. Veo on Imaging at 58% ±9.5) are not clearly statistically significant, so 'consistently preferred' is overstated.

The technical novelty is incremental: the framework largely assembles existing components (Eulerian flow, SAM, hash-grid encoding, Kabsch, WonderWorld-style scene expansion), and the bidirectional opacity blending is a simple heuristic rather than a principled physical model.

Several important details are missing or vague, including the sequence length/temporal loop length, motion-field training/regularization, exact use of directional hints, and the meaning of 'FLAGS' in the framework figure.

The runtime comparison may be apples-to-oranges: 12s is per scene-expansion step, while baselines are often measured for full video generation; a multi-step expansion cost is not reported, and 12s per update is interactive but not real-time.
There is no broader societal-impact discussion and limited failure-case analysis, although the limitations section mentions rigid-body motion as out of scope.

strengths: Targets an underexplored and relevant problem: interactive 4D world generation with environmental dynamics such as clouds, water, smoke, and fire, moving beyond static 3D scene reconstruction.
Proposes an explicit global 3D motion field rather than relying on expensive video-based optimization, which is a reasonable direction for efficient dynamic scene generation.
The geometry-aware alignment is computationally lightweight (Kabsch + short refinement), and the hash-based motion field is built on standard but effective Instant-NGP-style encoding.
The bidirectional propagation with an opacity scheduler is a simple and empirically useful design: the ablation reports hole-rate reduction from 9.8% to 0.9%.

The paper includes quantitative VBench results, a GPT-based physical-realism metric, a 2AFC human preference study, and several ablations, showing strong temporal-quality scores and runtime advantages over 4D-scene baselines.

The supplementary material provides useful additional details, runtime breakdowns, motion-consistency metrics, and qualitative examples, which improve clarity and reproducibility relative to the main paper alone.
weaknesses: The alignment formulation is technically questionable. It estimates a single global rotation and uniform scale for all scene-flow vectors, assuming that every current 3D velocity is a globally rotated/scaled version of the previous velocity. This cannot hold for spatially varying environmental motion (e.g., water waves, smoke, clouds, fire) in different regions and directions. The method also matches correspondences by rounded reprojection to the same pixel, which is brittle and sparse; non-overlapping regions bypass alignment and are simply accumulated, breaking global consistency.

The learned motion field is trained only with an MSE loss on sparse scene-flow samples, with no smoothness, divergence-free, or physical regularization. A hash-grid MLP can therefore extrapolate arbitrarily in unobserved regions, so the central claim of stable propagation across the scene is not substantiated. No independent motion-field accuracy or generalization metric is reported.

Bidirectional propagation updates only Gaussian centers, not covariances, orientations, opacity, or appearance. Fluid-like environmental dynamics should deform and rotate primitives, not merely translate them; this may explain the artifacts visible in ablation images and the failure on rigid-body motion acknowledged in the supplement.

The evaluation protocol is weak and not fully comparable. Video-generation baselines do not construct persistent 3D scenes, and 4D-scene baselines are not interactive. VBench scores are saturated and differ little (e.g., Motion Smoothness >0.99 for almost all methods), and the GPT-based PhysReal metric is inconsistently described as GPT-5.5 in the main paper and GPT-4o in the supplement, making it difficult to reproduce or trust.

The claimed interactivity is not convincingly supported. The reported 12-second update latency (9s expansion + 3s motion) is not real-time or low-latency interaction. More importantly, the human interactivity study shows LivingWorld rated lower than the baseline on usability (5.65 vs 5.80), controllability (5.90 vs 6.20), usefulness (6.00 vs 6.20), and average (5.85 vs 5.93), directly contradicting the claim that the additional 4D controls preserve convenience.

Novelty is incremental. The pipeline builds heavily on existing components: WonderWorld-style interactive scene expansion, Eulerian flow prediction from 3D Cinemagraphy, Kabsch alignment, Instant-NGP hash encoding, and 4D Gaussian rendering. The core combination is useful but the individual contributions are mostly straightforward engineering adaptations, not a substantial technical advance.

Ablations are insufficient to validate the key design choices. The alignment ablation compares only against naive scene flow and 3D-MOM, using self-defined metrics (MCA, FMV, global cosine, magnitude ratio) that may favor the proposed global alignment. There is no sensitivity analysis for depth noise, number of correspondences, user-hint sparsity, motion magnitude, or different motion categories.

Reproducibility and attribution are concerning. The citation for Veo 3.1 [37] does not match the listed reference, references include future-dated/unverifiable entries, and the system depends on proprietary or unreleased components such as Veo 3.1 and GPT-5.5 without clear access details or code release.

The scope is narrower than claimed. The paper claims interactive 4D world generation but only demonstrates environmental dynamics in four categories, with object-centric rigid motion shown to introduce geometric distortions. Broader 4D world dynamics (humans, articulated objects, complex interactions) are left entirely to future work.

strengths: The paper introduces a timely and well-motivated task: interactive 4D world generation with environmental dynamics such as clouds, water, smoke, and fire from a single image, going beyond static 3D scene generation.

The proposed system combines an explicit 3D scene representation with a global motion field, enabling coherent motion across progressively generated and expanded views while supporting user interaction.

The geometry-aware alignment module is a clear technical contribution: it consolidates independently estimated scene-flow samples using Kabsch alignment plus lightweight refinement, and the ablation shows improved local and global motion consistency over naive accumulation and 3D-MOM optimization.

The hash-based continuous motion field and bidirectional motion propagation with an opacity scheduler are well-designed for efficiency and coverage. The ablation and boundary-hole analysis show a large reduction in holes (9.8% to 0.9%) and stable temporal behavior without expensive video-based refinement.

Quantitative results are competitive and often best on temporal and physical-plausibility metrics (Motion, Flicker, PhysReal), and the runtime of ~12 seconds is substantially lower than the minutes-to-hours required by the compared video-generation and 4D-scene baselines.

The human preference study with 95 participants and the interactivity study provide useful complementary evidence beyond automatic metrics. The paper also honestly acknowledges limitations, especially that rigid object-centric motion is outside the primary scope.

The manuscript is generally clear, with informative figures, a readable method section, and helpful supplementary implementation details. Judged primarily as an Applied/Systems contribution, the paper convincingly demonstrates a working interactive 4D world-generation framework.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is moderate: the framework integrates several existing components (WonderWorld-style scene expansion, Eulerian flow prediction, SAM, depth estimation, hash encoding, and Kabsch alignment). The core advance is mainly the system design and the alignment/motion-field combination rather than a fundamentally new algorithm.

The experimental comparison is complicated by the lack of direct baselines. Video-generation methods do not maintain an explicit 3D scene, and 4D scene methods are not designed for interactive expansion with motion hints, so the current comparisons are only approximate. Some gains over strong baselines are also small.

The motion field is a stationary, time-independent velocity field, and bidirectional propagation explicitly loops the scene back toward its initial configuration. This may limit genuinely long, non-cyclic environmental dynamics and can introduce rewind or ghosting behavior that is not fully evaluated.

Important technical details are underspecified: it is not entirely clear how the 2D Eulerian flow is lifted into 3D scene-flow vectors in world coordinates, nor how the global rotation-and-scale alignment remains valid for spatially varying local motion across a large scene.

The evaluation relies on GPT-based PhysReal and VBench metrics; there is an inconsistency between the main paper (GPT-5.5-based PhysReal) and the supplementary material (GPT-4o-based metrics), which weakens reproducibility and confidence in the physical-plausibility claims.

Reproducibility would be stronger with a code or model release statement. The paper uses publicly available pretrained models, but the complete interactive system and evaluation protocol are not fully released or detailed enough for exact replication.

Real-time interactivity is not fully demonstrated: 12 seconds per update may be acceptable for a prototype but is still noticeable latency, and the user study reports slightly lower usability, controllability, and usefulness than the baseline interface, despite the positive framing.

The paper claims broad support for dynamic worlds, but object-centric and rigid-body motion is only briefly demonstrated and can introduce geometric distortions. The broader dynamic-world claims are therefore not fully supported beyond environmental motion.
